title: Same-Letter Run With K Edits
statement:
Given a string s of uppercase letters and an integer k, you may change at most k characters of s, each to any uppercase letter.

Return the length of the longest stretch of consecutive characters that can be made all the same letter.

examples.why: Change the J in "KKJK" to get four Ks (or the K in "JKJJ"). Adding k to the longest existing run would give only 2 + 1 = 3.
No edits allowed and no two neighbours match.
The stretch cannot be longer than the string. Unused edits do not add length.

constraints: s holds uppercase English letters only
hints: For a fixed stretch, how many edits does it need? Think about which letter you would keep.
A stretch of length L whose most common letter appears f times needs L − f edits. It is valid when L − f ≤ k. That is a window condition.
Grow the window on the right. If it needs more than k edits, slide its left edge one step. You only care about the largest frequency ever seen, so it never has to go down.

explain.intuition:
For any stretch, the cheapest plan keeps its most frequent letter and rewrites the rest. A stretch of length L whose top letter appears f times needs L − f edits. So we want the longest window with L − f ≤ k, a classic sliding window with a 26-slot count array.

The neat part: the window never needs to shrink, only slide. Once you have found a valid window of length L, you only care about windows longer than L. A longer valid window needs a bigger top frequency than any seen so far. So keep maxFreq as the largest frequency ever seen, even if it is stale for the current window. When the window is too costly, move the left edge by one so the length stays the same. The window grows only when a new record frequency makes a longer window valid.
steps: Keep a count per letter, a left edge start = 0, and maxFreq = 0.
For each end: count s[end] and update maxFreq with its count.
If (end − start + 1) − maxFreq > k, the window needs too many edits: uncount s[start] and move start one step.
The window length end − start + 1 is now the best length found so far; record it.
pitfalls: Taking the longest existing run and adding k. In "KKJKJJ" the edit can join two runs, and in "ZZZZ" with k = 3 the result would be longer than the string.
Counting distinct letters instead of the top frequency. A window is valid based on how many characters differ from its most common letter, not how many kinds there are.
Using while to shrink and recomputing the true max frequency each time. It is correct but needs a 26-slot scan per step. The non-shrinking window gives the same answer with less work.

solutions.title: Every start, extend with counts
solutions.idea: For each start, extend right while tracking the top frequency. Every valid stretch is checked.

solutions.title: One window per target letter
solutions.idea: Fix the letter you will keep. Then the window may hold at most k other letters: an easy window. Repeat for each letter that appears.

solutions.title: One window with the record frequency
solutions.idea: Keep the largest letter count ever seen. When the window needs too many edits, slide it instead of shrinking it. It only grows when a new record appears.
solutions.py:
class Solution:
    def longestWithEdits(self, s: str, k: int) -> int:
        count = [0] * 26
        start = max_freq = best = 0
        for end, ch in enumerate(s):
            c = ord(ch) - 65
            count[c] += 1
            max_freq = max(max_freq, count[c])
            if end - start + 1 - max_freq > k:
                # too many edits: slide the window right by one, keeping its length
                count[ord(s[start]) - 65] -= 1
                start += 1
            best = max(best, end - start + 1)
        return best

followups: Return the stretch itself, not just its length.
